note: One MO forms per atomic orbital, so ten 2s orbitals give 10 MOs. The 10 × 2 = 20 valence electrons fill all 10 at two per MO, within the 2s-only model the prompt sets up. A full band conducts only because the empty 2p band overlaps it, by the Day 12 p.18 rule (like Zn on p.23).
Twelve 4s orbitals give 12 MOs. The 12 valence electrons fill the lowest 6 at two per MO, so 6 are empty (a half-filled band, like Na's).

Both clusters' 3s MOs span nearly the same energy range, but the 60-atom cluster puts 60 levels there instead of 6, so the HOMO–LUMO spacing shrinks (Day 12 p.19–21). Hückel chain check, N = 6 vs 60: bandwidth 3.60 vs 4.00 |β|, gap 0.89 vs 0.10 |β|.

Li's half-filled band and Ca's filled band overlapping an empty one both meet the Day 12 p.18 conductor rule. Ge has a small gap, so it's a semiconductor (a metalloid on p.16); quartz has a large gap, so it's an insulator.

Heating lifts more electrons across the gap into the empty band and leaves vacancies in the filled band, so both bands carry current and conductivity rises. The Day 12 p.24 'T up' sketch keeps the same gap, so option 3 is wrong: the gap doesn't close.

As has 5 valence electrons to Si's 4, so each As adds one extra electron, held in a donor level just below the conduction band and easily promoted into it. That makes it n-type (Day 12 p.25 shows the same thing for P).

B has 3 valence electrons, one fewer than Si, which creates an acceptor level just above the valence band. Valence electrons that move into it leave positive holes, and electrons hopping between holes carry the current (p-type; textbook §18.5, Day 12 p.25 Ga acceptor).

Textbook values: P donor about 4 kJ/mol, Ga acceptor about 7 kJ/mol, Si gap 106 kJ/mol. Diamond's gap is the large insulator gap of Day 12 p.24, about 5.5 eV ≈ 530 kJ/mol (a value from outside the course data, not needed for the order).

Per photon, E = (106 × 10³ J/mol)/(6.022 × 10²³ /mol) = 1.760 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, and λmax = hc/E = (6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)(2.998 × 10⁸ m/s)/(1.760 × 10⁻¹⁹ J) = 1.1285 × 10⁻⁶ m ≈ 1.13 × 10³ nm (3 sig figs). That is near-infrared, beyond the 750 nm edge of the visible range.

Why one extended solid conducts and another doesn't (Cu's partly filled band vs diamond's large gap) is a band-theory question. SiH₄'s shape is VSEPR, O₂'s magnetism is a one-molecule MO question, and silicon's bond count is a Lewis question.

One MO forms per atomic orbital combined (Day 12 p.7), so 100 3s orbitals give 100 MOs, and the 100 valence electrons fill the lower 50. Option 0 double-counts: a bonding/antibonding pair comes from two AOs, not two MOs per AO.

Sb (group 15, 5 valence electrons) replaces Ge (group 14, 4), so each Sb donates an extra electron from a donor level just below the conduction band: n-type. A trace dopant doesn't turn Ge into a metal, and the course lists Sb as a metalloid (Day 12 p.16).
One MO per atomic orbital: 20 atoms × (one 3s + three 3p) = 80 MOs. The 20 valence electrons fill only 10 of them.
